newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Gazprom seen as tempting to investors and taxman.
newsitem.headline: Gazprom seen as tempting to investors and taxman.

text.p: The vast reserves of Russia's Gazprom, the world's biggest gas company, should ensure success of an international share offering but are tempting to a cash-strapped government worried about big tax arrears, analysts said on Monday.

As lead managers of Gazprom's planned offering of American depositary shares announced preliminary pricing of the sale, Russia's tax authorities froze the assets of two more Gazprom subsidiaries, complaining of big unpaid bills, Prime-Tass news agency said.
"They have an incredible amount of reserves and a distribution system as well," said James Fenkner, head of research at CentreInvest Securities in Moscow.
"The major financial risk for Gazprom near-term is the federal budget deficit and that it would continue to be used to fill the gap."
The government, eager to boost budget revenue, has declared war on tax debtors.

Gazprom admits it owes 15 trillion roubles ($2.77 billion), although it says it is owed three times as much, and some analysts have said the authorities may be squeezing the company to scare other big debtors into paying up.

Russia's biggest company by market capitalisation, it controls 23 percent of global gas reserves and supplied 21 percent of Western Europe's demand in 1995 out of its production of 560 billion cubic metres (19.78 trillion cu ft) of gas.
Gazprom supplies gas through pipelines linking Russia to various nations, including Germany, Italy, France, the Czech Republic and Poland. More are on the drawing board.
"What is really important is that they have the infrastructure to get the assets to market," said Renaissance Capital energy analyst James Bunch.

Gazprom has nearly 70 subsidiaries, giving it upstream and downstream strength. It also owns stakes in banks and, in July, snapped up a 30 percent stake in Russia's leading commercial television network.
Investors have long been eager to take a slice of Gazprom, which is 40 percent state-owned, but its 23.6 billion shares are highly illiquid because of company restrictions on selling them.
The shares were quoted at $0.354 on the Russian Trading System on Monday.

Investment banks Morgan Stanley and Dresdner Kleinwort Benson said on Monday that 23.7 million American Depositary Shares in Gazprom would be offered at a preliminary price of between $14 and $16 each.
Each ADS represents 10 ordinary shares.

"They can probably get a pretty healthy response because it is unique among Russian companies, if not global energy companies," said Bunch. But he said the $14-16 ADS price -- equivalent to $1.40-1.60 a share -- would not please investors.
Gazprom, with its headquarters in a gleaming glass tower in Moscow, also has political clout. Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Fuel and Energy Minister Pyotr Rodionov used to work there.
"That is a huge benefit for the company. It is still a very political environment in terms of getting access to natural resources and business in general," Bunch said.
But the government, struggling to meet the terms of a $10 billion International Monetary Fund loan programme, is keen to boost tax revenues and has turned the spotlight on Gazprom.
Company chairman Rem Vyakhirev said in a letter to parliament last week that the government had frozen some assets of its biggest production unit to claw back tax arrears.
Prime-Tass said on Monday that tax inspectors had frozen the accounts of two more Gazprom units in central and northern Russia, which it said owed about one trillion roubles.
No comment was immediately available from Gazprom.
Fenkner said Gazprom was quite inefficient, with net sales per worker only six percent of the equivalent at Exxon Corp.
But he said CentreInvest had calculated Gazprom's reserves could last 80 years without new finds.
"It is not going to take 80 years to clean up the company." ($1=5422 Rouble)
